'''''Coleus madagascariensis''''', [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Plectranthus madagascariensis''''', is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Lamiaceae]] that is native to [[southern Africa]] and [[southeastern Africa]].<ref name=POWO_446072-1/> Its common names include, '''thicket coleus''', '''Madagascar coleus''', and '''candle plant'''.<ref name=sanbi>{{cite web |url=http://pza.sanbi.org/coleus-madagascariensis |title=''Coleus madagascariensis'' |last1=Harrower |first1=Adam |last2=Notten |first2=Alice |date=June 2020 |publisher=South Africa National Biodiversity Institute |access-date=2 November 2024 }}</ref>

==Description== 
[[File:Plectranthus madagascariensis 2019-12-13 6350.jpg|thumb|left|Leaf detail]]
It is a [[herbaceous]], fragrant, semi-[[succulent]], multibranched plant with a sprawling growth habit that becomes a dense rambling [[subshrub]] reaching 1m high, where it will root as the branches touch the ground. The young branches are square in cross-section with opposite leaves. 

The dark green leaves are broadly [[Ovate (botany)|ovate]] with 3-7 pairs of rounded teeth, somewhat hairy both above and below and 35-40 mm in length. The cultivar 'Lynne' features variegated leaves that have splashes of creamy-white to pure white margins on them.<ref name =sanbi/><ref>[https://www.plantbook.co.za/coleus-madagascariensis/ Coleus madagascariensis]  Plantbook.co. Retrieved 2 November 2024.</ref> Crushed leaves create an [[oregano]]-like aroma.<ref>[https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/flora/6/6/6659 Coleus madagascariensis 'Variegated Mintleaf'] by the [[National Parks Board]]. Retrieved 2 November 2024.</ref>

===Inflorescence===
The small, white to [[mauve]] [[inflorescence]] is a terminal upright [[raceme]], reaching 125 mm in length, supporting 4-6 flowers at each [[Plant stem|node]]. Each flower is 7-18 mm long, arranged in whorls, two-lipped and tubular in a spike-like inflorescence. The [[calyx (botany)|calyx]] is 3 mm long, extending to 5 mm after the flower falls and grasps the brown seeds or nutlets which are 1mm in diameter. Blooming occurs in early autumn to late autumn.<ref name =sanbi/>

==Distribution==
It is native to [[South Africa]], [[Swaziland]], [[Eswatini]], [[Mozambique]], [[Mauritius]] and [[Réunion]], but not [[Madagascar]].<ref name=POWO_446072-1>{{cite web |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:446072-1 |title=''Coleus madagascariensis'' (Pers.) A.Chev.. |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Board of Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=7 October 2022 }}</ref> Growing in the seasonally [[Tropical and subtropical dry broadleaf forests|dry tropical]] biome, it is found in shaded subtropical brushes, on dry rocky outcrops and forest edges. It can survive extreme drought by wilting and remaining in a state of weak, semi-[[dormancy]] until rainfall occurs again.<ref name =sanbi/>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Plectranthus madagascariensis var madagascariensis 1.jpg|thumb|'Variegated Mintleaf']]
Propagation can easily be made by [[cuttings (plants)|cuttings]] in the summer, where no [[rooting hormone]] is required. The plant thrives in lightly shaded areas. Its cultivar 'Variegated Mintleaf' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web |title=''Plectranthus madagascariensis'' 'Variegated Mintleaf' (v) plectranthus 'Variegated Mintleaf' |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/49223/Plectranthus-madagascariensis-Variegated-Mintleaf-(v)/Details |date=2021 |publisher=The Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=26 April 2021 |quote=Synonyms; ''Plectranthus madagascariensis'' 'Variegata', ''Plectranthus coleoides'' 'Variegatus' }}</ref> 

The plant is safe from pests because of the [[pungent]] leaf fragrance, therefore it is not predated by herbivorous animals. Though [[larval]] caterpillars of moths and butterflies can flourish on the plant's leafy parts, thereby disturbing the leaves.<ref name =sanbi/>

===Uses===
It has been used in [[traditional medicine]] to treat coughs, colds and [[scabies]]. The pungent leaves and branches are sometimes hung in homes or rubbed on window sills to repel flies.<ref name =sanbi/>

==Taxonomy==
This species was first acquired in 1775 by [[Philibert Commerson]] in [[Mauritius]] or Réunion, though it should also have been known from Madagascar (due to its specific name, ''madagascariensis'' meaning ‘of Madagascar’). It was initially placed in the genus [[Ocimum]] and transferred to [[Plectranthus]] in 1832. [[Molecular]] studies on Plectranthus and closely related genera resulted in the alteration of the genus in 2019 and the restoration of the genus Coleus.<ref name =sanbi/>
